units.text: We'll follow a request across three trust boundaries: the public A P I, the function and the data store. At each boundary, identify what should be allowed, who enforces that decision, and what evidence helps verify it.

The gateway verifies caller access; the function still needs least-privilege permission to data. Check the remaining risk afterwards. Even an authenticated request can be inappropriate if the authorization is broader than the job needs.

Imagine an approved application role is suspected of accessing an unusual volume of data. Narrow the role and resource permissions so it can read only what its job requires. Review applicable network and encryption policy separately.

Use the configured object activity records and any supported GuardDuty signal to establish the affected scope. Route the evidence to the incident owner. If the response is justified, use an approved scoped containment action and verify required work still succeeds.

The automation role should trust the service that actually runs it. In this example, the bucket A P I is put public access block, but the I A M permission is S three colon put bucket public access block. Scope that permission to the named bucket the automation owns.

Use supported policy conditions, and consider a permissions boundary as a maximum, not a grant. Test the allowed change and the denied case. Log execution and verify the resulting bucket posture instead of assuming the finding is resolved.

External access analysis flags supported access outside the trusted zone. Unused access findings help review stale permissions; policy validation checks a policy for errors and warnings. Those capabilities answer different questions.

A finding means the analyzed policy permits a path; it doesn't prove anyone used it or automatically deny it. Confirm whether the sharing is intended, narrow it if necessary, and verify updated analysis and authorized access.
